analysis.title: Investing in American Resilience
key_insights: GMO argues American reindustrialization will be an important driver of investment returns over the next decade, and that standard U.S. equity indexes are poorly positioned to capture it because of their global, technology-heavy composition.
GMO launched the Domestic Resilience Strategy in October 2025, an actively managed approach that is also offered as the Domestic Resilience ETF.

Three forces are named as driving reindustrialization: public policy (CHIPS Act, Inflation Reduction Act, One Big Beautiful Bill, steel tariffs, defense appropriations, export controls), corporate policy (reshoring and friendshoring after COVID supply chain disruption) and defense policy (rare earth stockpiling and expanded missile, drone and autonomous weapons capacity).
Less than 60% of S&P 500 company revenue comes from the U.S., a share that has declined for years. As of 6/30/2026, the chart shows 58% U.S., 25% developed ex-U.S. and 17% emerging markets.

Industrials, Energy and Materials together made up more than 25% of the S&P 500 in the late 1990s and are now under 15%, so the index is light in companies that benefit most directly from reindustrialization.
The S&P 500 returned nearly 15% per annum in the decade ending 2025, led by technology.

The strategy screens for companies with a majority of revenue from the U.S. and groups them into four categories: Manufacturing & Automation, Transportation & Logistics, Energy & Materials, and Defense.
Stock selection rests on quality (picks-and-shovels business models with durable moats) and value (avoiding securities priced for perfection).
GMO says it currently finds the best valuation opportunities in industrial companies with limited or indirect exposure to the AI buildout, and says the active approach lets it rotate as that changes.

sector_views.rationale: Manufacturing & Automation names such as engineering and construction firms, equipment rental and automation companies are seen as direct beneficiaries of reindustrialization.
Domestic manufacturing at many U.S. sites increases demand for rail and trucking, replacing ocean shipping of finished goods.
Domestic oil, gas and aggregates producers supply the inputs to industrial growth, and supply near industrial production is limited.
Conflict is increasing globally, technology is changing warfare and China's military is growing, which supports U.S. defense contractors.
The report says tech growth has crowded out industrial companies in the S&P 500, and GMO currently finds better value in industrials with limited AI exposure.

risk_factors: Reindustrialization is a slow, long-term process still in its early stages.
Volatile tariff policies and export control battles add uncertainty to corporate planning.
Securities priced for perfection are prone to underperformance, which is why the report stresses valuation.
The report notes the market is increasingly short-term oriented, so a decade-long theme may get little investor attention.
charts_described: Exhibit 2 (as of 6/30/2026) shows S&P 500 sales exposure at 58% U.S., 25% developed ex-U.S. and 17% emerging markets, with the U.S. share trending down.
Exhibit 3 (as of 6/30/2026) plots the combined S&P 500 weight of Industrials, Energy and Materials, which is below 15% today.
geopolitical: China's 2001 WTO entry and its state support for manufacturing (cheap debt, grants, subsidized electricity, forced technology transfer) shifted production offshore.
China's control of the rare earth supply chain and its willingness to use it as a chokepoint prompted U.S. defense responses including stockpiling.
The Russia-Ukraine and Middle East conflicts have raised energy costs and forced expensive shipping re-routing.
Volatile tariff policy under the second Trump Administration and export control disputes over rare earths and semiconductors add risk to corporate supply chains.

theme_stances.key_argument: Public, corporate and defense policy together will have a slow but significant long-term impact on America's industrial capacity.
theme_stances.evidence: American reindustrialization will be an important driver of investment returns in the decade ahead

theme_stances.key_argument: The S&P 500 is remarkably global and light in the industrial companies that benefit most from reindustrialization.
